parties.appellant_or_petitioner: Lahore High Court, Bahawalpur Bench, Bahawalpur in C.Rs. Nos.618 & 619 of 2011/BWP] Saad Younis & 6 others

statutes_cited: Sections 188 and 189 of the Contract Act, 1872
holding: Consequently, these appeals are allowed. The judgment dated 30.03.2012 passed by the Lahore High Court, Bahawalpur Bench, in Civil Revision Nos.618 and 619 of 2011 is set aside, while the judgments and decrees dated 29.07.1986 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge, Rahim Yar Khan, and 25.07.2011 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Rahim Yar Khan, respectively, are restored. paragraphs.text: SHAHID BILAL HASSAN, J- The controversy arises out of two consolidated suits concerning agricultural land measuring 100 kanals and 4 marlas situated in Mouza Pallu Shah, Tehsil Rahim Yar Khan. The appellant, Ghulam Bari, instituted a suit on 14.12.1978 seeking possession of the suit property and recovery of its produce, asserting that although he was owner of the land, the respondents had unlawfully dispossessed him. During the pendency of that suit, respondent Muhammad Younas instituted a separate suit on 08.03.1979 for specific performance on the basis of an agreement to sell dated 20.01.1979, allegedly executed on behalf of the appellant by his attorney, Ahmad Din, pursuant to a registered power of attorney dated 31.08.1977. Both suits were consolidated and, after recording evidence, the learned Senior Civil Judge, Rahim Yar Khan, vide common judgment and decree dated 29.07.1986, dismissed the appellant's suit for possession and decreed the respondent's suit for specific performance. The litigation thereafter underwent a protracted procedural course. The appeals preferred by the appellant were initially dismissed but were repeatedly remanded by the High Court on different occasions for fresh decision in accordance with law. Ultimately, the learned Additional District Judge, Rahim Yar Khan, vide judgment dated 25.07.2011, upheld the judgment and decree of the trial court. Aggrieved, the appellant filed Civil Revision Nos. 618 and 619 of 2011, which were allowed by the Lahore High Court, Bahawalpur Bench, through judgment dated 30.03.2012. The High Court set aside the concurrent judgments of the courts below, held that the alleged power of attorney had not been proved in accordance with law and further observed that, in any event, it did not authorize the attorney to enter into an agreement to sell on behalf of the principal. Consequently, the suit for specific performance was dismissed while the appellant's suit for possession was decreed. Aggrieved thereby, the respondents have preferred the present appeal.

Learned counsel for the appellants contended that the High Court gravely erred in upsetting the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the trial court and affirmed by the first appellate court while exercising revisional jurisdiction. It was argued that the registered power of attorney dated 31.08.1977 stood duly proved through cogent oral and documentary evidence, including the testimony of the petition writer, the Sub-Registrar, Ahmad Din, and other corroborative evidence demonstrating that Ahmad Din had acted as the appellant's attorney by redeeming the Agricultural Development Bank loan from the earnest money received under the agreement to sell. Learned counsel further submitted that the subsequent execution of the deed of revocation (Ibtal Nama) unequivocally acknowledged the existence of the power of attorney. It was lastly contended that the authority to sell necessarily encompassed the authority to execute an agreement to sell, and the High Court erred in adopting an unduly restrictive interpretation of the instrument. The impugned judgment, therefore, being contrary to the record and settled principles governing revisional jurisdiction, warrants interference.

Conversely, learned counsel for the respondents supported the impugned judgment and submitted that the execution of the power of attorney had not been proved in accordance with law, particularly in view of the testimony of Nazir Ahmad, the identifying witness before the Sub-Registrar, who categorically denied having identified Ghulam Bari at the time of its execution. It was argued that the very foundation of Muhammad Younas's suit for specific performance consequently collapsed. Learned counsel further maintained that even assuming the power of attorney had been validly executed, it merely authorized the attorney to administer and sell the property and did not expressly empower him to enter into an agreement to sell, which creates independent contractual obligations binding upon the principal. It was, therefore, submitted that the High Court rightly reversed the erroneous findings of the courts below and no case for interference by this Court is made out.

Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and examining the record, the following questions arise for determination: (i) whether the High Court, while exercising revisional jurisdiction, was justified in reversing the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the trial court and affirmed by the first appellate court regarding the due execution and proof of the registered power of attorney dated 31.08.1977; and (ii) whether the authority conferred upon Ahmad Din under the said power of attorney to sell the suit property included, either expressly or by necessary implication, the authority to execute the agreement to sell dated 20.01.1979, thereby entitling Muhammad Younas to the decree for specific performance.

At the very outset we note that the learned High Court reversed the concurrent findings of the trial court and the first appellate court primarily on the premise that the execution of the registered power of attorney was not proved in accordance with law, as Nazir Ahmad (D.W.4), who had identified the executant before the Sub-Registrar, subsequently stated that he had identified Ahmad Din as Ghulam Bari at the instance of one Arshad. With respect, we find ourselves unable to subscribe to this view.

Before adverting to the appreciation of evidence, it is pertinent to note that the document in question is a registered power of attorney, to which the law attaches a statutory presumption of due execution and authenticity1. Article 95 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 mandates that the Court shall presume every document purporting to be a power of attorney and authenticated by the competent authority to have been duly executed. In Mst. Iqbal Bibi v. Kareem Hussain Shah (2024 SCMR 1233) this Court reiterated that a registered power of attorney "enfolds a presumption of truth and genuineness" and the burden lies upon the party alleging fraud to rebut such presumption by satisfactory evidence. Likewise, in Anjuman-e-Khuddam-ul-Qur'an, Faisalabad v. Lt. Col. (R) Najam Hameed (PLD 2020 SC 390) it was held that a registered document carries sanctity and can only be displaced by strong and cogent evidence and this same principle was reaffirmed in Abdul Aziz v. Abdul Hameed (2022 SCMR 842). In the present case, the registered power of attorney was produced from proper custody and its execution was supported not merely by its registration but also by the testimony of the petition writer (D.W.6), the then Sub- Registrar (D.W.5), Ahmad Din himself (D.W.7), and the documentary evidence showing that, acting as attorney, Ahmad Din redeemed the Agricultural Development Bank loan admittedly obtained by Ghulam Bari by utilizing the earnest money received under the agreement to sell. Significantly, Ghulam Bari himself subsequently executed an Ibtal Nama revoking the very same power of attorney on 21.02.1979. Had no such power of attorney ever existed, there would have been no occasion to execute a formal deed of revocation. This subsequent conduct constitutes a strong circumstance corroborating the defendants' case regarding its prior execution. 1 Muhammad Siddique (deceased) v. Mst. Noor Bibi (deceased) (2020 SCMR 483), Abdul Razaq v. Abdul Ghaffar (2020 SCMR 202); Muhammad Idrees v. Muhammad Pervaiz (2010 SCMR 5); Rasool Bukhsh and another v. Muhammad Ramzan (2007 SCMR 85)

Although the learned High Court placed decisive reliance upon the statement of Nazir Ahmad (D.W.4), the trial court was not bound to accept every part of his testimony in isolation. It is a settled principle that the testimony of a witness is to be appreciated as a whole and the court is entitled to accept those parts of the evidence which inspire confidence while rejecting the remaining parts in the light of the surrounding circumstances and the documentary record. In the present case, the testimony of the petition writer, the Sub-Registrar, Ahmad Din, the contemporaneous conduct of the parties and the subsequent execution of the Ibtal Nama furnished ample corroboration for the execution of the registered power of attorney. The learned High Court, therefore, erred in treating the isolated statement of Nazir Ahmad as conclusive while disregarding the cumulative effect of the remaining evidence.

The statement subsequently made by Nazir Ahmad before the trial court merely created a conflict in the oral evidence, which the trial court, after recording evidence first-hand, resolved in favour of the defendants. That finding was affirmed by the first appellate court. It is settled that revisional jurisdiction under Section 115, C.P.C. is supervisory and not appellate. It is confined to correcting jurisdictional defects, material irregularity, illegality or findings suffering from perversity arising from misreading or non-reading of evidence. It does not permit a fresh appraisal of evidence merely because another view is possible. The trial court had the advantage of recording oral evidence and assessing the demeanour of witnesses, while the first appellate court independently concurred with those findings. In the absence of perversity or patent illegality, the High Court was not justified in substituting its own view. The High Court, however, reassessed the entire evidence as if exercising first appellate jurisdiction and substituted its own opinion merely because another view was possible. Moreover, the learned High Court did not identify any material piece of evidence which had either been misread or ignored by the courts below, nor did it point out any jurisdictional error or perversity in the concurrent findings warranting interference in revision. This approach is plainly contrary to the settled law. In Sultan Muhammad and another v. Muhammad Qasim and others (2010 SCMR 1630), this Court held that concurrent findings of fact, if not based upon misreading or non-reading of evidence and not suffering from any illegality or material irregularity affecting the merits of the case, are not open to interference in revisional jurisdiction. Therefore, such reappraisal in the instant case transgressed the settled limits of revisional jurisdiction. We, therefore, hold that the registered power of attorney stood duly proved.

The second reason assigned by the High Court is that although the attorney may have been authorised to sell the property, he was not expressly empowered to enter into an agreement to sell, and therefore the agreement dated 20.01.1979 was beyond the scope of his authority. Again, we are unable to agree.

This principle finds statutory recognition in Sections 188 and 189 of the Contract Act, 1872, which embody the doctrine of implied and incidental authority. Once a principal confers authority upon an agent to accomplish a particular act, the authority extends to every lawful thing necessary for accomplishing that act together with every act ordinarily incidental thereto, unless the instrument itself expressly restricts the agent's powers. A power of attorney, therefore, is to be construed reasonably so as to give effect to the intention of the principal as gathered from the instrument as a whole. Where an attorney is expressly authorised to alienate immovable property, such authority ordinarily comprehends the authority to negotiate its terms and execute the antecedent agreement to sell, which constitutes the contractual foundation of the eventual conveyance. To hold that an attorney may execute the final sale deed but lacks authority to execute the preceding agreement to sell would render the authority to sell commercially impracticable and legally incongruous, defeating rather than advancing the intention of the principal as expressed in the instrument.

The interpretation adopted by the learned High Court would lead to an anomalous result. If an attorney is competent to execute the final conveyance transferring ownership of immovable property, it would be incongruous to hold that he lacks authority to execute the antecedent agreement to sell, which merely embodies the contractual consensus culminating in that conveyance. Such a restrictive construction would render the authority to sell commercially impracticable and would defeat, rather than advance, the manifest intention of the principal as expressed in the instrument.

Nothing has been brought on record to demonstrate that the power of attorney expressly prohibited Ahmad Din from entering into a contract for sale or otherwise restricted the manner in which the authority to sell was to be exercised. Once the execution of the power of attorney stood established and the authority to sell was conferred, the execution of the agreement to sell in furtherance thereof fell within the ordinary scope of such authority.

The conduct of the parties further fortifies this conclusion. Ahmad Din admittedly received Rs.35,000/- as earnest money and utilized the same for redemption of Ghulam Bari's outstanding bank liability. The balance sale consideration remained available for payment at the time of execution and registration of the sale deed. The evidence concurrently appreciated by the courts below also establishes the readiness and willingness of Muhammad Younas to perform his part of the contract. The refusal to complete registration emanated from Ghulam Bari after cancellation of the power of attorney and not from any default attributable to Muhammad Younas.

The judgments of the trial court and the first appellate court reveal a comprehensive appreciation of both oral and documentary evidence extending over several witnesses and exhibits. The findings returned therein are neither arbitrary nor unsupported by the record. Both Courts undertook an exhaustive appraisal of the oral and documentary evidence and recorded concurrent findings after assigning cogent reasons. None of those findings has been shown to suffer from misreading, non-reading or perversity. The distinction between appellate and revisional jurisdiction has repeatedly been emphasized by this Court. In Muhammad Sarwar and others v. Hashmal Khan and others (PLD 2022 SC 13) and Mst. Zarsheda v. Nobat Khan (PLD 2022 SC 21), it was held that a revisional court cannot interfere merely because another view of the evidence is possible; interference is permissible only where the findings recorded by the courts below are perverse, suffer from jurisdictional error, or are founded upon misreading or non-reading of material evidence. Similarly, in Salamat Ali and others v. Muhammad Din and others (PLJ 2023 SC 8), this Court observed that a revisional court cannot substitute its own findings simply because it considers them more plausible than those recorded by the subordinate courts. More recently, in Mst. Farzana Zia and others v. Mst. Saadia Andaleeb (2024 SCMR 916), it was reiterated that where two courts have concurrently reached the same conclusion after evaluating the relevant evidence, the High Court ought not to revisit such crystallized findings unless they are shown to be legally unsustainable or productive of manifest injustice. The High Court not identify any perversity, jurisdictional defect or misreading/non-reading of evidence in the concurrent findings; rather, it merely preferred a different appreciation of the same evidence and adopted a restrictive interpretation of the power of attorney. Such an approach falls outside the permissible limits of revisional jurisdiction

For the foregoing reasons, we hold that the learned High Court was not justified in reversing the concurrent findings of the courts below. Accordingly, we hold that the learned High Court misdirected itself both in law and in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. The registered power of attorney dated 31.08.1977 stood duly proved; Ahmad Din was competent to execute the agreement to sell dated 20.01.1979 on behalf of Ghulam Bari; and Muhammad Younas successfully established his entitlement to the equitable relief of specific performance. The impugned judgment, by reappreciating the evidence in revision and by assigning an unduly restrictive construction to the registered power of attorney, cannot be sustained in law.

Consequently, these appeals are allowed. The judgment dated 30.03.2012 passed by the Lahore High Court, Bahawalpur Bench, in Civil Revision Nos.618 and 619 of 2011 is set aside, while the judgments and decrees dated 29.07.1986 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge, Rahim Yar Khan, and 25.07.2011 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Rahim Yar Khan, respectively, are restored. The parties shall bear their own costs. JUDGE JUDGE Announced in open Court at Lahore on 10.08.2026. JUDGE “Approved For Reporting” M.A. Hassan
